title: Development and analytical evaluation of a microneutralization cytopathic effect assay for human adenovirus type 55-specific neutralizing antibodies

analysis.research_question_and_background: Reliable quantification of neutralizing antibodies (nAb) against human adenovirus type 55 (HAdV-55) is critical for the evaluation of emerging vaccine candidates.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study established and analytically validated a microneutralization assay based on cytopathic effect (MN-CPE) as a scalable alternative for HAdV-55-specific nAb quantification.
analysis.methods: Comparative performance analysis was conducted between the MN-CPE assay and the plaque reduction neutralization test (PRNT), assessing dilution linearity, relative accuracy using high-, middle-, and low-titer reference sera, and negative-control acceptance ranges.
analysis.main_results: Both assays maintained high dilution linearity, with coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.988 for MN-CPE and 0.9926 for PRNT, and demonstrated acceptable responses across the dynamic range. The MN-CPE assay provided a distinct statistical advantage over PRNT by defining a negative-control acceptance range.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the MN-CPE assay is analytically comparable to PRNT and serves as a practical, relatively high-capacity alternative for HAdV-55 neutralization testing in clinical and preclinical vaccine research.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a scalable and efficient method for quantifying HAdV-55-specific neutralizing antibodies, which is essential for evaluating vaccine candidates and advancing clinical and preclinical research.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study demonstrates high analytical comparability between MN-CPE and PRNT, with evidence strength supported by rigorous validation and testing across multiple parameters, though limitations related to generalizability beyond HAdV-55 were not explicitly addressed.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed and validated a microneutralization cytopathic effect assay (MN-CPE) as an alternative to the plaque reduction neutralization test (PRNT) for quantifying neutralizing antibodies against human adenovirus type 55 (HAdV-55). The MN-CPE assay demonstrated high dilution linearity (R2 = 0.988) and comparable performance to PRNT (R2 = 0.9926), with the added advantage of defining a negative-control acceptance range. Both assays successfully detected HAdV-55-specific nAbs in immunized cynomolgus macaques without cross-reactivity to other HAdV types. The MN-CPE assay offers a practical, high-capacity alternative for HAdV-55 neutralization testing in clinical and preclinical vaccine research.

title: Preclinical Safety Evaluation of a Replication-Defective Canine Adenovirus Type 2 Vector-Based SARS-CoV-2 Vaccine Candidate in Murine Models

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study was needed because pre-existing immunity to common human adenovirus serotypes can limit vaccine effectiveness, and comprehensive preclinical safety data for canine adenovirus type 2 (CAV-2) vector-based vaccine platforms remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study evaluated the safety profile of a replication-defective CAV-2 vector-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate in BALB/c mouse models, with mice receiving intramuscular prime-boost immunisations at low, moderate, or high vaccine doses, alongside control groups, and monitored longitudinally up to Day 72.
analysis.methods: The vaccine was expressed and propagated in AD293 cells; mice were clinically assessed at days 0, 7, 21, 42, and 72; biochemical analyses evaluated liver and kidney function; hematological parameters were assessed via complete blood counts; and body temperature and weight changes were monitored.
analysis.main_results: Biochemical and haematological parameters remained within physiological reference ranges across all dose groups and timepoints, with no dose-related deviations; body temperatures remained normal, and body weights increased normally without abnormal gain or loss.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the replication-defective CAV-2-vectored SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate was well tolerated and did not demonstrate evidence of systemic toxicity, supporting its translational potential as an alternative adenoviral vector-based vaccine platform.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the continued development of CAV-2 as a vaccine delivery platform, with implications for future vaccine design where pre-existing immunity to human adenoviruses is a concern.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the limited scope of safety endpoints, as the study did not include histopathological, vector persistence, or shedding evaluations, which are warranted to support further development.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the preclinical safety of a replication-defective canine adenovirus type 2 (CAV-2) vector-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate in BALB/c mice. Mice received intramuscular prime-boost immunisations at low, moderate, or high doses, alongside control groups, and were monitored for 72 days. Clinical assessments, biochemical analyses, hematological parameters, body temperature, and weight changes showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, tissue or haematological toxicity, or systemic toxicity. The vaccine candidate was well tolerated, supporting CAV-2's potential as an alternative adenoviral vector-based vaccine platform. However, further studies with additional safety endpoints, including histopathological and vector persistence evaluations, are needed.

title: Live attenuated vaccines alone or in combination with an adenovirus-based vaccine protect mice lacking IFN-γ against pneumonic plague

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study evaluated the protective efficacy of live-attenuated vaccines alone or in combination with an adenovirus-based vaccine against pneumonic plague in wild-type and interferon-γ knockout mice.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used wild-type and interferon-γ knockout mice challenged with lethal intranasal doses of Yersinia pestis CO92 to assess vaccine protection.
analysis.methods: Vaccines included triple deletion mutants of Y. pestis CO92 (LMA and LMP) and a trivalent adenoviral vector-based vaccine (Ad5-YFV), with immune responses measured through humoral and cellular assays.
analysis.main_results: Protection of 80 to 100% was observed in vaccinated mice, with robust humoral and cellular immune responses, and superior lung immunity in both wild-type and interferon-γ knockout mice using a prime-pull strategy.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that IFN-γ may not be required for protection against pneumonic plague by these vaccines, and combining live-attenuated and adenovirus-based vaccines augmented systemic and local immune responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that these vaccines could provide long-lasting immunity against pneumonic plague, particularly in immunocompromised individuals lacking IFN-γ.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is high due to robust protection and immune responses observed, though the study was limited to mouse models and may not fully translate to humans.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the protective efficacy of live-attenuated vaccines (LMA and LMP) alone or combined with an adenovirus-based vaccine (Ad5-YFV) against pneumonic plague in wild-type and interferon-γ knockout mice. The vaccines provided 80-100% protection, with robust humoral and cellular immune responses. Notably, IFN-γ knockout mice showed better B cell activity and activated T cells, and IFN-γ depletion did not reduce protection, suggesting IFN-γ may not be required for vaccine efficacy. The prime-pull strategy enhanced lung immunity and provided full protection in mice lacking multiple interferon receptors. Combining vaccines augmented systemic and local immune responses, potentially offering long-lasting immunity against pneumonic plague.

title: Evaluation of transduction properties and vaccine efficacy of a simian adenovirus type 25-based vector.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Although human adenovirus serotype 5 (Ad5) is widely used as a vaccine vector due to its high transduction efficiency, pre-existing immunity to Ad5 in many people reduces vaccine efficacy. To address this limitation, simian Ad vectors, such as ChAdOx1 and ChAdOx2, have been explored as alternative vaccine platforms.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study aimed to characterize the gene transduction efficiency, tissue distribution, and immunogenicity of an SAd25-based vector in comparison with those of the Ad5 vector following various routes of administration.
analysis.methods: The study compared intravenous, intramuscular, and intranasal administration routes of the SAd25 vector and the Ad5 vector, evaluating gene transduction efficiency, tissue distribution, and immunogenicity.
analysis.main_results: Compared with intravenous administration of the Ad5 vector, intravenous administration of the SAd25 vector showed distinct biodistribution patterns, including reduced liver accumulation and predominant expression in the lung. The SAd25 vector was not inhibited by human serum, whereas the Ad5 vector was inhibited, indicating that the SAd25 vector can evade pre-existing Ad immunity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings provide essential insights into the biological characteristics of the SAd25 vector, supporting its potential as a safe and effective vaccine vector that can evade pre-existing immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The SAd25 vector's ability to evade pre-existing immunity and its distinct biodistribution patterns make it a promising alternative to Ad5-based vaccines, particularly for intranasal administration which induced a more rapid antigen-specific antibody response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not evaluate long-term safety or efficacy in humans, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the limited scope of the study and the need for further validation in clinical settings.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the transduction properties and vaccine efficacy of a simian adenovirus type 25 (SAd25)-based vector compared to the widely used human adenovirus serotype 5 (Ad5) vector. The SAd25 vector demonstrated distinct biodistribution patterns, with reduced liver accumulation and predominant lung expression following intravenous administration. Notably, the SAd25 vector was not inhibited by human serum, allowing it to evade pre-existing immunity, which is a significant limitation of Ad5-based vaccines. While intramuscular administration of SAd25 induced lower antibody production than Ad5, gene expression was localized to the administration site. Intranasal administration of SAd25 induced a more rapid antibody response in serum compared to Ad5, with comparable antibody production in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. These findings support the potential of SAd25 as a safe and effective vaccine vector, particularly for intranasal delivery.

title: Spatiotemporal distribution of Escherichia coli and fecal and non-fecal pathogens in the urban surface water system of Amsterdam

analysis.research_question_and_background: Understanding the microbial quality of urban surface water, particularly pathogens dynamics, is crucial for determining public health risks from recreation and for developing effective monitoring strategies in water-centric cities like Amsterdam.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We monitored six locations along Amstel River and inner canals between May and October 2023 using ultrafiltration sampling and qPCR to quantify Escherichia coli, four fecal, and three non-fecal pathogens.
analysis.methods: Spearman's correlations were conducted to explore relationships between E. coli, pathogens, water temperature, and rainfall.
analysis.main_results: Human adenovirus appeared in 17 of 36 samples (0.2–2.6 log10 copies/100 mL), most frequently near the wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) and correlated with rainfall (p < 0.01), suggesting runoff or effluent influences.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrates that human adenovirus occurrence in Amsterdam's surface water is spatially and temporally variable, with higher detection near WWTP and correlation with rainfall, indicating potential environmental contamination sources.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Future monitoring frameworks should integrate selected fecal and non-fecal pathogens alongside traditional indicators to improve assessments of urban microbial water quality, incorporating microbial source tracking markers may further enhance source attribution while balancing feasibility and cost.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence strength is moderate due to limited sample size and temporal scope, though the consistent detection patterns and statistical correlations provide robust insights into pathogen dynamics.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the spatiotemporal distribution of Escherichia coli and fecal and non-fecal pathogens in Amsterdam's urban surface water system between May and October 2023. Using ultrafiltration sampling and qPCR at six locations, researchers found that human adenovirus was detected in 17 of 36 samples (0.2–2.6 log10 copies/100 mL), with higher frequency near the wastewater treatment plant and significant correlation with rainfall (p < 0.01). Other pathogens like Campylobacter, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Legionella pneumophila showed varying spatial and temporal patterns. The study highlights limitations of E. coli as an indicator for these pathogens and recommends integrating multiple pathogen indicators into future monitoring frameworks to better assess urban water quality and public health risks.

title: Adenoviral E3/49K: CD45-targeted immune evasion and therapeutic potential

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) cause a broad spectrum of diseases, ranging from mild respiratory and gastrointestinal infections to severe, sometimes even fatal illness in immunocompromised individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Species D adenoviruses represent the largest group, possibly driven by strong evolutionary pressure, particularly within the highly variable early transcription unit 3 (E3), which encodes immunomodulatory proteins.
analysis.methods: Among these, E3/49K is unique to species D and utilizes a particularly intriguing immunomodulatory strategy.
analysis.main_results: It is a heavily glycosylated transmembrane protein that undergoes proteolytic shedding to release the soluble ectodomain (sec49K), the only known secreted HAdV protein.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Both the membrane-anchored and soluble forms target the leukocyte-specific receptor-like protein tyrosine phosphatase CD45, a key regulator of immune cell activation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: E3/49K binds CD45 with high affinity via two domains, inducing dimerization and inhibiting its phosphatase activity, thereby suppressing activation of T, B, and NK cells.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The species specificity and potent immunomodulatory function of E3/49K underscore its role in adenoviral adaptation and highlight its potential for therapeutic immunosuppression and cancer therapy.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the immunomodulatory function of the E3/49K protein in human adenoviruses, particularly species D. It highlights the unique strategy of E3/49K, which is a heavily glycosylated transmembrane protein that can shed to release a secreted form. The protein targets CD45, a key regulator of immune cell activation, and its interaction with CD45 inhibits phosphatase activity, suppressing T, B, and NK cell activation. These findings suggest that E3/49K plays a significant role in adenoviral adaptation and may have therapeutic potential for immunosuppression and cancer treatment. The study provides foundational insights into the molecular mechanisms of immune evasion by HAdVs, which could inform future research and applications in virology and immunotherapy.

title: A field-deployable immunofluorescence chip for adenovirus monitoring in groundwater systems

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rapid field detection of human adenoviruses in groundwater remains a critical technological gap, particularly for riverbank filtration systems exposed to extreme weather and contamination events.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we present the VIRUMEX chip, a field-deployable platform that captures and detects adenovirus proteins through immunofluorescence using antibody-functionalized 3D Sepharose beads integrated into a disposable flow-through microfluidic cartridge.
analysis.methods: Powered by a compact peristaltic pump, the system autonomously processes groundwater and yields fluorescence-based readouts in light intensity unit (LIU) within 4-8 h, enabling near-real time semi-quantitative pathogen surveillance.
analysis.main_results: Laboratory tests produced a clear detectable signal at 0.129 ng/mL (1000 LIU) for adenovirus hexon protein, and field deployment in the Erpe River catchment produced above-background fluorescence (800 LIU) in river water, providing proof-of-concept evidence with positive signal under real riverbank filtration conditions, while groundwater samples remained negative under the tested conditions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: By providing an on-site, rapid, and operationally simple detection method, the VIRUMEX chip provides an additional on-site virus screening prototype alongside qPCR and isothermal approaches and offers a promising prototype for integrating virus monitoring into groundwater safety frameworks which needs some further optimizations before it can be regarded as a fully validated detection tool.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The VIRUMEX chip enables near-real time semi-quantitative pathogen surveillance in groundwater systems, offering a promising prototype for integrating virus monitoring into groundwater safety frameworks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study provides proof-of-concept evidence with positive signal under real riverbank filtration conditions, but the VIRUMEX chip needs further optimizations before it can be regarded as a fully validated detection tool, indicating moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the critical technological gap in rapid field detection of human adenoviruses in groundwater systems, particularly for riverbank filtration systems exposed to extreme weather and contamination events. The researchers developed the VIRUMEX chip, a field-deployable platform that captures and detects adenovirus proteins through immunofluorescence using antibody-functionalized 3D Sepharose beads integrated into a disposable flow-through microfluidic cartridge. The system autonomously processes groundwater and yields fluorescence-based readouts in light intensity units within 4-8 hours, enabling near-real time semi-quantitative pathogen surveillance. Laboratory tests showed a detectable signal at 0.129 ng/mL for adenovirus hexon protein, and field deployment in the Erpe River catchment produced above-background fluorescence in river water, though groundwater samples remained negative. The VIRUMEX chip offers a promising prototype for integrating virus monitoring into groundwater safety frameworks, though it requires further optimization before being fully validated.
